Get educated, because the real product is learning how to learn. Work for someone long enough to see how taxes, politics, and promotions actually work. Then get laid off (I did, from the Ottawa Hospital) and realize it's the best thing that ever happened to you.

The message I care most about is the decade nobody talks about: from 22 to 32, with no kids and no mortgage, I woke up at 5, went to bed at 8, worked six or seven days a week, and built my first company from zero to 45 employees across Canada before selling it inside ten years, just like the plan said. That decade put the rest of my life in a place where I can run multiple businesses, hire people, and dictate my own time with three young boys at home. If you're in your 20s and thinking about starting something: scrap everything and put in the reps now. I can mentor you 20 or 30%. The other 70% has to come from you.

episodes.title: If I Lost Everything Today: My Exact First 90 Days
episodes.description:
Laid off at 24. Financially free with an eight-figure net worth by 34. If I lost all of it tomorrow, here's exactly what I'd do in my first 90 days — and it starts with knocking on doors, not building a website.

Days 1–30: Sell before you build. Use Claude or ChatGPT to research the ten most boring businesses your region actually needs, filter for what you can do without a licence, pick one, and go sell it door to door. No equipment. No website. Not a dollar spent. If 100 doors say no, do 50 more. If they still say no, move to the next idea.

Days 31–60: Service them yourself. Five customers minimum, and you do the work — not a subcontractor. This is where you learn your real cost of goods sold, how money actually reaches you, and what the customer's face does when you deliver.

Days 61–90: Rinse, repeat, raise your price. Same script, new neighbourhood, ten customers instead of five, $125 instead of $100. Now you're not guessing — you're compounding.

The mistake most people make is working backwards: buy the equipment, build the site, spend the money, then look for customers. There's never been a better time to be an entrepreneur — the research is at your fingertips. You just have to do.

1) Review your financials and compare them to prior years

5) Follow up until you have closure in writing
6) Do what CRA wants, then stay on top of it so it doesn’t snowball later

If you’re a business owner and you want a clear, calm process for handling CRA reviews without spiraling, this episode will help.
